subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 geography question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Interactions between human and physical processes

questions.q: What is the name for the huge slabs of the Earth's crust that slowly move around on the mantle?
questions.explain: The crust is cracked into tectonic plates that drift a few centimetres a year on the hot, flowing mantle. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur where these plates meet.

questions.q: Two plates move apart and magma rises to make new sea floor at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. What type of boundary is this?
questions.explain: When plates diverge (pull apart) and new crust is created from rising magma, it is a constructive boundary. Destructive boundaries push together; conservative boundaries slide past.

questions.q: Water freezes in a crack in a rock, expands, and breaks a piece off — but the piece stays exactly where it fell. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Freeze-thaw breaks rock down in place with no movement, so it is weathering (physical weathering). Erosion is when material is worn away AND carried off.

questions.q: Which of these rocks is an example of a sedimentary rock, formed from layers pressed together?
questions.explain: Limestone is sedimentary, formed from layers of material compacted over time. Granite is igneous (cooled magma) and marble is metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure).

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the difference between weather and climate?
options: Weather is the 30-year average; climate is today's conditions
Weather is short-term and local; climate is the long-term average over about 30 years
They mean exactly the same thing
Climate only describes rainfall, weather only describes temperature
questions.explain: Weather is what the atmosphere is doing right now in one place; climate is the average weather over roughly 30 years. A single cold day is weather, not evidence about climate.

questions.q: What is the main way humans are speeding up climate change today?
options: Burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide
The end of the last Ice Age
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps extra heat. This enhanced greenhouse effect is driving recent, rapid warming beyond natural change.

questions.q: Roughly when did the last Ice Age end, after covering much of Britain in ice?
questions.explain: The last Ice Age ended around 11,700 years ago. Climate has changed naturally throughout Earth's history due to factors like the Earth's orbit, the Sun's output and volcanic activity.

questions.q: The Sun heats the sea and turns liquid water into water vapour that rises. This process is called:
questions.explain: Turning liquid water into vapour with heat is evaporation. Condensation is the opposite (vapour cooling into clouds) and precipitation is water falling as rain, snow or hail.

questions.q: What is the term for water vapour released into the air by plants through their leaves?
questions.explain: Transpiration is water vapour released by plants. Evaporation is from water surfaces like seas and lakes; both add vapour to the air, which then condenses into clouds.

questions.q: How does covering land with concrete and buildings change the water cycle?
options: More water soaks into the ground
More water runs off quickly, raising flood risk
questions.explain: Concrete stops water soaking in, so rain runs off the surface quickly into rivers. This raises flood risk — an example of humans changing a physical system.

questions.q: You find a wide valley with steep sides and a flat floor — a clear 'U' shape. What most likely carved it?
questions.explain: Glaciers carve broad, steep-sided U-shaped valleys through plucking and abrasion. Rivers cut narrower V-shaped valleys, so valley shape is a clue to what shaped it.

questions.q: At the coast, waves erode a headland into a cave, then an arch, which collapses to leave a tall pillar of rock. What is this pillar called?
questions.explain: The erosion sequence is cave to arch to stack to stump. A spit is a coastal deposition landform and a moraine is glacial debris.

questions.q: Which three things does a river do to material as it flows from source to mouth?
questions.explain: A river erodes (wears away), transports (carries) and deposits (drops) material along its course, building landforms such as waterfalls, meanders and flood plains.

questions.q: What does 'urbanisation' mean?
options: A growing share of people living in towns and cities
questions.explain: Urbanisation is the increasing proportion of people living in towns and cities. It is often driven by rural-to-urban migration for jobs, education and services.

questions.q: A person moves from a village to a city because the city has more jobs and better schools. These attractions are examples of:
questions.explain: Pull factors attract people TO a place (jobs, schools, healthcare). Push factors, like a lack of jobs, drive people AWAY from where they currently live.

questions.q: Which of these is a development indicator geographers use to compare quality of life between countries?
options: The speed a tectonic plate moves
The height of the tallest mountain
questions.explain: Life expectancy is a development indicator, along with GDP per person, literacy rate and the HDI. These measure how wealthy, healthy and educated a country is.

questions.q: What does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine into a single score?
questions.explain: The HDI combines income (wealth), health (life expectancy) and education into one number, giving a broader picture of development than money alone.

questions.q: Which set of energy resources is entirely NON-renewable (finite)?
questions.explain: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels — non-renewable resources that run out and release carbon dioxide when burned. Solar, wind, tidal and hydro are renewable.

questions.q: Which of these are the four main types of natural resource studied in KS3 geography?
questions.explain: The four key natural resources are energy, water, food and minerals. They are spread unevenly across the world, which affects trade, wealth and development.

questions.lo: Interactions between human and physical processes
questions.q: A city clears a hillside of trees and covers it in concrete. After heavy rain, what is the most likely result?
options: Less run-off and lower flood risk
More water soaks into the ground
More run-off and a higher flood risk
No change to the water cycle
questions.explain: With trees gone (less transpiration and interception) and concrete stopping water soaking in, rain runs off quickly into rivers — a human action increasing flood risk in a physical system.
